title: Cheapest Passes for Set Days
statement:
You plan to visit a climbing gym on certain days of the year, given as a strictly increasing array days with values from 1 to 365.

The gym sells three passes, with prices in costs: costs[0] buys a 1-day pass, costs[1] a 7-day pass and costs[2] a 30-day pass. A pass bought on day d covers d and the following days up to d + 6 (7-day) or d + 29 (30-day).

Return the least total you can pay so that every day in days is covered. Prices are not guaranteed to grow with the length of the pass.

examples.why: One 7-day pass for days 1–7 (9) and a 1-day pass for day 20 (2). Eight daily passes would cost 16.
Here the 7-day pass is cheaper than a single day, so buy two of them even though each covers only one visit.
Visits are spread out, so 7-day passes cover only two each (40 total) and daily passes cost 24. One 30-day pass wins.

hints: Think about the first uncovered visit. Some pass must cover it, and buying that pass on that very day is never worse than buying it earlier.
So at each visit you have three choices, and each choice jumps you forward to the first visit the pass does not cover. That is a recursion with overlapping subproblems.

Let best[d] be the cheapest cost to cover all visits on days ≥ d. Then best[d] = best[d+1] if d is not a visit day, else the minimum of costs[0] + best[d+1], costs[1] + best[d+7], costs[2] + best[d+30].

explain.intuition:
Look at the earliest visit that is not covered yet. Some pass has to cover it, and starting that pass on exactly that day covers as much of the future as possible. So there are only three decisions to make, and after each one the problem is the same problem on a later suffix of the calendar.

That gives a small DP over days. Walk the calendar from day 365 down to day 1. A day you do not visit costs nothing extra, so it copies the next day's value. A visit day takes the cheapest of the three passes plus whatever covering the rest costs from where that pass ends. A greedy rule such as "always the best price per day" fails because prices can be in any order, as the second example shows.
steps: Put the visit days in a set, and make an array best of size 366 + 30 filled with 0.
If d is not a visit day, set best[d] = best[d + 1].
Otherwise set best[d] = min(costs[0] + best[d + 1], costs[1] + best[d + 7], costs[2] + best[d + 30]).
pitfalls: Assuming longer passes are always cheaper per day, or that a 1-day pass is always the cheapest single purchase.
Off-by-one on coverage: a 7-day pass bought on day 1 covers days 1 to 7, so the next uncovered day is 8.
Indexing past 365 when d + 30 runs off the end. Pad the array, or treat those entries as 0.

complexity.time: O(365) = O(1) for a fixed year; O(W) for a calendar of W days

solutions.title: Plain recursion over visits
solutions.idea: At visit i try all three passes and recurse on the first visit each one does not cover. Exponential without memo.

solutions.title: DP over the calendar
solutions.idea: best[d] = cheapest cover for all visits on days ≥ d. Non-visit days copy best[d + 1]; visit days try the three passes.

solutions.title: DP over visits with forward pointers
solutions.idea: Index the DP by visit instead of by calendar day, so the cost depends on the number of visits, not the length of the year.

followups: The calendar is now ten years long with a few hundred visits. Which of the two DPs do you pick, and why?
Also return which passes to buy. What do you store next to each best value?
